analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal rules on coal ash disposal, banning unlined ash ponds and requiring utilities to guarantee cleanup costs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to a House subcommittee in April 2021 with 19 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, it received no hearing or markup and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced the EPA to write tougher rules for state programs that regulate coal combustion residuals — the toxic ash left over from burning coal. It would have banned continued use of unlined ash ponds, required utilities to post bonds guaranteeing cleanup costs, limited toxic dust, and given nearby residents public hearings and a real say in permits. It never advanced past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near coal ash ponds and disposal sites — often low-income communities and communities of color — would gain cleaner groundwater, dust controls, air monitoring, and replacement drinking water if wells are contaminated. Well owners, state regulators, and the EPA would also gain stronger tools, and taxpayers would be protected from footing cleanup bills because utilities would have to post financial guarantees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities living near coal ash sites

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the continued operation of unlined coal ash impoundments and denies closure permits that would leave ash in contact with groundwater or in floodplains — the main ways ash poisons drinking water.

Requires utilities to post a surety bond or irrevocable letter of credit covering closure, post-closure care, cleanup, and accident liability, with no allowance for self-bonding — so residents and taxpayers are not left holding the bill if an operator walks away or goes bankrupt.

Requires meaningful public participation — notice, comment, and hearings — in every permit decision, limits permits to five-year terms, and requires the EPA to hold a public hearing before approving any state program, giving affected residents real standing.

Caps fugitive toxic dust at 35 micrograms per square meter with required air monitoring, expands groundwater testing to detect more contaminants, requires cleanup beyond facility boundaries, and obliges operators to supply alternative safe drinking water to well users whose water is contaminated.

Requires owners of closed coal ash sites to survey and publicly record their locations, so buried ash dumps cannot be built over or forgotten, and directs the EPA to review state permit programs every five years instead of every twelve and to fix deficiencies within 180 days.

analysis.who_pays: Coal-burning utilities that own coal ash impoundments would bear the costs of closing unlined ponds, posting financial guarantees, monitoring, and remediation. Some of those costs would likely be passed to their electricity customers through rates, and states would face tighter EPA oversight of their permit programs.

drawbacks.text: The cleanup, closure, bonding, and monitoring requirements would cost utilities substantially, and those costs would likely flow to electricity customers through rates, including in regions where coal plants serve lower-income ratepayers.

Denying any closure permit that leaves ash in contact with groundwater could force utilities to excavate and relocate millions of tons of ash from existing ponds, an expensive and disruptive undertaking at sites across the country.
The bill overrides state discretion by dictating federal minimum program requirements, five-year permit terms, and speedier EPA review, which some state regulators would view as reduced flexibility.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and fall on the people most exposed: safer groundwater, dust limits, and a guaranteed payer for cleanups near coal ash sites. The costs are real but conventional for environmental regulation — closure and bonding expenses that utilities would spread across their customer base. The bill was a straightforward tightening of existing waste-disposal law, not a radical restructuring, and its main defect is one of process: it never even received a hearing, so the trade-offs were never publicly tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its environment subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Ensuring Safe Disposal of Coal Ash Act on April 8, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Five days later, on April 13, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change — the last action the bill ever received.
Nineteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

The bill would have required the EPA to revise its coal ash regulations to ban unlined impoundments, require bonds covering closure and cleanup, mandate public hearings and five-year permit terms, and review state programs every five years instead of twelve.
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of coal ash impoundments — chiefly coal-burning electric utilities — are better off, because they continue operating under the existing rules without the closure, bonding, monitoring, and remediation obligations the bill would have imposed. The communities near those sites gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-burning utilities that own ash ponds

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 19 Democratic cosponsors.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 19 were Democrats, with no Republican support.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change from April 2021 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill also died in a committee controlled by the same party without ever reaching a vote, so the decisive inaction was intra-party.

industries.note: These companies own most coal ash impoundments and would have had to close unlined ponds, post bonds covering closure and accidents, monitor groundwater, remediate contamination, and record buried ash sites publicly. Their interest in avoiding those costs ran directly against the health interests of communities near ash sites, and the bill's death leaves them operating under the looser existing framework.

The bill required financial assurance solely in the form of surety bonds or irrevocable letters of credit, banning cheaper self-bonding, which would have created a new stream of demand for these financial products. A modest, incidental gain tied to a public-protection mechanism.
